findings.consequence: An admin or superuser sending a crafted cursor with a negative offset to the audit-log endpoint gets an unhandled exception and a 500 response. The "advanced" feature does not work, and the offset clamp is weakened for the is_prev path in BasePaginator.
findings.explanation: With optimized_pagination=true and enable_advanced_features=True, a client-supplied cursor with a negative offset (for example cursor=0:-5:0) takes the negative-offset branch. Cursor.from_string accepts negative offsets via int(bits[1]). The branch then runs queryset[start_offset:stop] with a negative start. Django querysets do not support negative indexing and raise an error, so the comment claiming the ORM handles negative slicing is wrong. If the slice did not raise, it would bypass the normal max(0, offset) clamp. The same mistake appears in BasePaginator.get_result, which now passes a negative offset through for is_prev cursors. The change adds nothing that makes this work.
findings.title: Negative cursor offset is passed to Django queryset slicing, which raises

findings.consequence: A replay with more than one page of segments sends duplicated error log lines to Seer, and in chronological order they are wrong. The generated summaries are therefore inaccurate for multi-page replays.
findings.explanation: The endpoint passes the full error_events list to analyze_recording_segments through functools.partial, and paginate calls it once per page of segment metadata. Each call runs gen_request_data with error_idx reset to 0. Every error that is not interleaved before an event in that page is emitted by the trailing loop, so on each page the log includes those errors again. Also, error timestamps come from nodestore in seconds, while replay event timestamps are normally in milliseconds. The comparison `error.timestamp < event.timestamp` is then nearly always true, so errors are placed before the first event instead of in chronological order.
findings.title: Error events are re-emitted on every paginated page and compared against ms timestamps

With an empty search, the sorted list is returned unfiltered, so is_segment, project_id and received are displayed. As soon as the user types any query, those attributes are removed. findings.consequence: A hung flusher keeps running after it is replaced, so two flushers handle the same shards. That can produce duplicate or conflicting segment flushes and leaks processes on every restart. On shutdown, join() does not terminate the child processes.
findings.explanation: The processes are created via mp_context = get_context("spawn"), so they are SpawnProcess instances. SpawnProcess subclasses BaseProcess, not multiprocessing.context.Process (which is what multiprocessing.Process refers to), so isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process) is False. The old code called self.process.kill() unconditionally. Now, when a flusher is unhealthy ("hang" cause, process still alive), kill() is skipped and _create_process_for_shards starts a second process for the same shards. The same check in join() skips terminate().
findings.title: Hung flusher processes are never killed: isinstance check against multiprocessing.Process fails for SpawnProcess

findings.consequence: After each restart or rebalance, the last processed message of every partition is consumed and processed again. If the topic has offset gaps, that partition's commits stall and a large backlog is reprocessed after restart.
findings.explanation: get_committable_offsets returns the highest processed offset N, and _commit_loop passes it straight to commit_function. Arroyo commit positions mean the next offset to consume (Message.committable is offset+1), so committing N leaves the already-processed message N as the resume point. The scan in get_committable_offsets also requires every integer from last_committed+1 upward to be in all_offsets. Any offset that is never submitted, such as a compaction or transaction-marker gap, makes the scan break there, and commits for that partition stop permanently.
findings.title: Commits last processed offset instead of next offset; stalls on offset gaps

findings.consequence: After a restart or rebalance, the last processed message of every partition is consumed and processed again. Uptime results can be handled twice.
findings.explanation: get_committable_offsets returns the highest fully processed offset, and _commit_loop passes that straight to commit_function. Arroyo commit callbacks expect the next offset to consume (BrokerValue.committable is offset+1). The tracker never adds one. So the committed position always points at an already processed message. The same value is stored as last_committed.
findings.title: Commits last processed offset instead of next offset (off by one)

findings.consequence: The test fails intermittently in CI depending on thread scheduling, which produces flaky failures unrelated to the code under test.
findings.explanation: The test submits 10 items to a pool whose worker threads are already running and consume items immediately. It then asserts stats["total_items"] > 0. get_stats() sums qsize(), and qsize() drops as soon as a worker calls get(). If the workers drain all 10 items between the last submit and get_stats(), the count is 0 and the assertion fails. Nothing in the test blocks the workers from running first. The result_processor does not block and only sets an event, so the window is plausible, especially under a loaded CI machine.
findings.title: test_stats_reporting asserts a racy queue depth and can fail intermittently

findings.consequence: The editor showed every resource as "all", but after one downgrade every other resource drops to "none" in the saved role.
findings.explanation: getResourcePermissionLevel reports "all" for every resource whenever `*.*` is present, even if no individual permissions are listed. toggleResourcePermissionLevel drops `*.*` at line 72 but does not expand it into individual permissions. If a role is stored with only `*.*`, lowering one resource leaves only the other individual permissions, which is an empty list. I did not check whether such roles exist in the data.

findings.consequence: Hosts can't confirm paid, requires-confirmation bookings from the list. Pending bookings with payment enabled and no payment rows get a confirm button that was previously hidden.
findings.explanation: The old confirm condition was `(isPending && !paymentAppData.enabled) || (paymentAppData.enabled && !!price && booking.paid)`. The refactor passes `showPendingPayment = paymentAppData.enabled && booking.payment.length && !booking.paid` into the context, and getPendingActions uses `(isPending && !showPendingPayment) || (showPendingPayment && booking.paid)`. Because showPendingPayment already requires `!booking.paid`, the second clause is always false. For a pending booking with payment enabled and already paid, the old code showed "confirm". The new code does not, since showPendingPayment is false so the first clause fires only when isPending is true, and it can wrongly fire in other states. Also, a pending booking with payment enabled but no payment rows now shows confirm, where the old code did not.
findings.title: Confirm action no longer shown for paid pending bookings (payment condition mis-translated)

findings.consequence: After a save, or any other refetch that changes the data, the editor unmounts and remounts. The user sees a flash of empty content and loses in-progress form state, such as the active tab and unsaved edits. It also causes redundant network refetches.
findings.explanation: The effect's cleanup invalidates and resets the atom event-type query. It was meant to run only on unmount or when `id` changed. The change added `eventTypeQueryData` to the dependency array, so the cleanup now also runs whenever the fetched data changes, for example after a save refetches the event type. `resetQueries` clears the cached data to undefined, and the component then hits `if (!eventTypeQueryData) return null`. That unmounts the whole `EventType` form, and the form remounts only once the refetch completes. I did not open the update mutation's code, so I am assuming it invalidates this query after a save.
findings.title: Adding eventTypeQueryData to effect deps resets the query and unmounts the form on every data change

findings.consequence: A CommonJS `require("@calcom/atoms")` or a tool that reads `main` resolves to a file missing from the published dist. This fails with module-not-found.
findings.explanation: The change adds `exports["."].require` and a top-level `main`, both set to ./dist/cal-atoms.umd.cjs. vite.config.ts builds with `formats: ["es"]`, so only the ES bundle is emitted. The scripts/dev-on.js dev helper normally patches in these same two fields and removes the `formats` restriction, so the committed package.json now carries the dev-only state while the build config does not.

findings.consequence: After a booking is reassigned, the denormalized routing form response rows show the new user id with the old user's name, email and avatar. Reports and filters that use these columns return wrong data until the response row is next refreshed.
findings.explanation: booking_update_trigger_for_routing_form fires on updates of "userId" (for example, when a booking is reassigned to another host). trigger_refresh_routing_form_response_denormalized_booking then sets "bookingUserId" = NEW."userId". It never updates "bookingUserName", "bookingUserEmail" or "bookingUserAvatarUrl". Those columns keep the previous host's values. The user-update trigger only fires when the users row changes, so nothing corrects them later.
findings.title: Booking update trigger changes bookingUserId without refreshing user name/email/avatar

findings.consequence: An attacker who knows only a user's email can log in as that user without their password. This works for any account that does not have 2FA enabled. For accounts that do have 2FA, an attacker holding only a TOTP code or backup code can log in without the password. This is a full authentication bypass of the credentials login flow.
findings.explanation: In authorize, the password is only verified when `user.password && !credentials.totpCode` (line 121). The identity-provider checks at lines 113 and 117 are also gated on `!credentials.totpCode`. Nothing later verifies the password. For a user without 2FA, the `else if (user.twoFactorEnabled)` branch is not entered, so the function goes straight to returning the user. A request with only a victim's email and any non-empty totpCode, such as "1", therefore authenticates. For a user with 2FA, the password is also skipped. The new backup-code branch (line 131) makes this worse. Sending email, any totpCode and one valid backup code passes without the password, because backup codes are only checked against the stored list. Non-CAL identity-provider users are also let through.
findings.title: Password check is skipped whenever totpCode is supplied, allowing login without a password

findings.consequence: A single-use backup code can authenticate more than once. An attacker who has a leaked code can race the legitimate user and both get in. Consumed codes can also be resurrected by a lost update. The 2FA single-use guarantee is broken. Existing 2FA users have NULL backupCodes and get MissingBackupCodes. That is a separate gap, and the code shown has no backfill or regeneration path for them.
findings.explanation: authorize reads user.backupCodes in the initial findUnique. It decrypts the value and checks indexOf in memory. It then sets the entry to null and writes the whole re-encrypted array back with an unconditional update keyed only by user id. There is no transaction, row lock, or compare-and-set on the previous ciphertext. Two concurrent logins that submit the same valid backup code both read the same array, both find the code, and both pass. The later write also overwrites the earlier one, so concurrent use of two different codes can restore a code that was already consumed.
findings.title: Backup code consumption is a non-atomic read-modify-write, so one code can be used by concurrent logins

findings.consequence: The Google `events.update` call goes out without a calendarId and fails, so the event update does not happen.
findings.explanation: The same no-op `find` is used in `updateEvent`, so `selectedCalendar` is undefined whenever `externalCalendarId` is falsy. The old code used the destination calendar's externalId.

findings.consequence: Cancelling an event without an explicit externalCalendarId, for example from the deleteCredential or payment flows, tries to delete from the wrong calendar ("primary"). The event stays on the intended destination calendar. `updateEvent` without an external id sends `calendarId: undefined` and the Google API call fails.
findings.explanation: The old fallback used `event.destinationCalendar?.externalId` when no `externalCalendarId` was passed. The change replaced it with `event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId`. That fallback only runs when `externalCalendarId` is falsy, so it searches for a calendar whose externalId equals undefined, null or an empty string. It effectively never matches, so the fallback always returns undefined. In `deleteEvent`, calls without an explicit calendar id now delete from "primary" instead of the booking's destination calendar. In `updateEvent`, `calendarId` becomes undefined.
findings.title: Google deleteEvent/updateEvent destination-calendar fallback can never match

findings.consequence: With team billing disabled (self-hosted), organizations are created with no slug, so org URLs and lookups by slug break. With billing enabled, the slug is set immediately instead of waiting for payment and verification, which skips the intended `requestedSlug` flow.

The change rewrote the first spread as `IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED ? { slug } : {}` and dropped the negation. The slug is now set when billing is enabled, which is also when `requestedSlug` is set. findings.consequence: Scheduled SendGrid emails for cancelled or rescheduled bookings are never cancelled, so attendees still get reminders. The first failure also aborts the loop, so the reminder rows are not deleted and the same failure repeats on every cron run.
findings.explanation: scheduleEmailReminders.ts imports the @sendgrid/client default export and calls client.request, but only calls sgMail.setApiKey (line 19). The only client.setApiKey call is in lib/reminders/emailReminderManager.ts:26. The handler's imports (customTemplate and emailReminderTemplate) do not import that module, and nothing in api/ references it. In the cron route's own process the client therefore has no API key, so the scheduled_sends cancel request is rejected with 401. The surrounding try/catch only logs the error.
findings.title: @sendgrid/client is never authenticated in the cron handler, so cancel requests fail

findings.consequence: Reminders for cancelled or rescheduled bookings are never cancelled at SendGrid or deleted from the database. Their emails can still be sent. A single failing reminder also blocks all the others on every run.
findings.explanation: The handler calls `sgMail.setApiKey` but never `client.setApiKey` for the separate `@sendgrid/client` singleton. `client.request` to `/v3/user/scheduled_sends` therefore depends on some other module having set the key. `emailReminderManager.ts` does set it, but this file doesn't import that module. If the key is unset, the first request is rejected. The whole loop sits in one try/catch, so that failure aborts the loop and is only logged. A bad or already-cancelled `referenceId` (it can be null) fails the same way and blocks every later reminder. The `prisma.delete` promises are lazy and are only awaited after the loop, so none of them run when the loop throws. Every cron run repeats this.
findings.title: SendGrid client used for cancel without an API key, and one failure aborts all cancellations

findings.consequence: Fixed hosts with multiple availability ranges per day, or with non-UTC timezones, will have valid slots removed from getSchedule results (the new check runs for every fixed and loose host). Slots that overrun the end of working hours are not rejected.
findings.explanation: The new working-hours block computes `end` identically to `start` (slot start, without adding eventLength), so the end bound is never checked against the slot's actual end. It uses `workingHours.find(...)` and treats any same-day entry that the slot falls outside of as "outside working hours". A user with split hours on one day (e.g. 09:00-12:00 and 14:00-17:00) has two entries for that day, so a 10:00 slot is outside the second entry and the function returns false. It also compares UTC hour/minute of the slot against startTime/endTime that are minutes in the organizer's timezone, so non-UTC organizers get slots wrongly dropped or kept.
findings.title: Working-hours check in checkIfIsAvailable rejects valid slots (end==start, any-range, UTC vs organizer tz)

findings.consequence: With credential sync on, callers receive parsed data without expiry fields, and the stored refresh token is replaced with the fake string "refresh_token". Zoom's refresh code (VideoApiAdapter.ts:119-124) writes that string into the credential's refresh_token. It also computes expiry_date as `Date.now() + undefined * 1000`, which is NaN. Later refreshes then send the bogus refresh token to the pro…
findings.explanation: `z.string().toString()` and `z.string().optional().toString()` are both "[object Object]", so the second computed key overwrites the first. The schema is therefore `{access_token: string, "[object Object]": unknown.optional()}`. It has no number-valued expiry rule and no catch-all. Zod's default strip mode removes every other field, including expires_in, expiry_date and refresh_token. The next step in parseRefreshTokenResponse then sees refresh_token as missing and sets it to the literal "refresh_token". This happens whenever credential sync is enabled and the endpoint is configured.
findings.title: minimumTokenResponseSchema computed keys are not wildcards; expiry fields are stripped and refresh_token is replaced by a placeholder

findings.consequence: In credential-sync mode, parsed refresh results lose expiry_date, expires_in and other fields. The stored credentials then look expired or lack expiry information, so tokens are refreshed repeatedly or integrations break. Callers such as the Zoom adapter that read newTokens.expires_in get undefined.
findings.explanation: The schema keys are `[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]`. Calling toString() on a Zod schema object returns "[object Object]". The schema therefore requires a literal property named "[object Object]" to be a number. The second computed key is the same string, so it overwrites the first and makes that property optional unknown. Real token responses (access_token, expires_in and so on) have no such property. When APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT are set, the second key overwrites the first in the object literal, so the number requirement is probably dropped. The schema is then effectively just access_token plus the default strip behaviour. That strips expires_in and other fields, because z.object strips unknown keys by default. The intended 'any numeric property is the expiry' and 'allow other properties' logic is not impleme…
findings.title: minimumTokenResponseSchema uses computed keys that stringify to "[object Object]", so credential-sync parsing always fails

findings.consequence: With credential sync on, hubspot credentials are overwritten in the DB with a serialized Response and a NaN expiry, which breaks the integration for that user. Google tokens never refresh and fail silently. Webex and zoom pass the Response to their own response handlers, so they were not shown to break.
findings.explanation: When credential sync is enabled, refreshOAuthTokens returns the fetch Response from the sync endpoint. It does not check the status, parse the body, or normalize the result. The non-sync branch returns whatever each caller's refresh function produces: the hubspot SDK token object, or the google `res` with `.data`. Hubspot types the result as HubspotToken and reads `.expiresIn` from it. A Response has no `expiresIn`, so `expiryDate` becomes NaN. The Response is then written to `credential.key` in the DB. Google reads `res?.data`, which is undefined on a Response, so `token.access_token` throws a TypeError. The surrounding catch treats any message other than invalid_grant as a no-op, so the refresh silently fails. The sync request also sends no auth header, so the endpoint cannot verify the caller. That last point comes from the code only, and I did not check what the endpoint requires.
findings.title: refreshOAuthTokens returns a raw fetch Response in sync mode, which hubspot and google misread as a token object

findings.consequence: Every construction of SalesforceCalendarService rejects `this.conn` after a successful token refresh, so Salesforce event and contact operations fail. If the import were added, the connection would still use the expired access token.
findings.explanation: The change adds `prisma.credential.update(...)` in getClient, but the file never imports `prisma`; grep finds only this usage. Because of that, once the refresh response is parsed, the call throws a ReferenceError (and a type error at compile time). Separately, the new token is persisted but the returned jsforce.Connection is still built with `credentialKey.access_token` (the old token) instead of `accessTokenParsed.data.access_token`. Also, `if (!accessTokenParsed.success)` is dead code, because parseRefreshTokenResponse throws on failure.
findings.title: Salesforce getClient uses undefined `prisma` and then connects with the stale access token

findings.consequence: If another reminder type later uses retryCount, this SMS cron would silently delete its pending reminders, including rows with scheduled=true that were already handed to the provider. The record would be lost without any cancellation.
findings.explanation: The new second OR branch in the deleteMany, `retryCount: { gt: 1 }`, has no `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` filter. The old delete was limited to SMS reminders. `retryCount` is a column on the shared WorkflowReminder table, so this SMS cron route now deletes any row with retryCount > 1, whatever its method (EMAIL or WHATSAPP). Only this handler increments the counter in the changed code, so no non-SMS rows are affected today. The scope is still wider than the handler's SMS-only intent.

findings.consequence: A blacklisted address in the request is still emailed even though it is not saved as an attendee. Existing attendees also get duplicate notifications. A mixed-case variant of a blacklisted address is both saved and emailed, which defeats the blacklist.
findings.explanation: The handler builds `uniqueGuests` by dropping guests who are already attendees or are in BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS. Only `uniqueGuests` are saved to the booking. The email step then calls `sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests)` with the original unfiltered `guests` input. Blacklisted addresses and existing attendees therefore still get the email. The blacklist check is also case-sensitive on the guest side. The blacklist is lowercased, but `guest` is not, so `Blocked@x.com` passes the filter.

findings.consequence: The error is fail-closed: a user can be wrongly denied access to a resource that has a colliding name/folder combination, for the cache TTL. It does not grant extra access. The cached entry also blocks a legitimate access that would otherwise be allowed.
findings.explanation: userPermDenialCacheKey builds the key as namespace + ".perm_" + userUID + "_" + action + "_" + name + "_" + parent. The fields are joined with '_' and not escaped. Resource names and folder UIDs can contain '_'. For example, name "a_b" with parent "c" and name "a" with parent "b_c" produce the same key. Check writes this key with permDenialCache.Set whenever a request is denied. It reads the key first and returns Allowed:false on any hit, before it looks at permissions. A denial for one resource can therefore be served as a denial for a different resource of the same user and action.
findings.title: Denial cache key joins fields with an unescaped '_', so different (name, folder) pairs can share a key

findings.consequence: Legacy storage writes can fail with `context canceled`, or can be skipped. Legacy storage then silently diverges from unified storage, even though Mode 3 is meant to keep writing to both. The failures are recorded only as legacy error metrics.
findings.explanation: Create, Delete, Update and DeleteCollection now run the legacy write in a goroutine. Each goroutine derives its timeout context from the request `ctx` with `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)`. The handler returns right after starting the goroutine, so the request context is cancelled and the derived context is cancelled with it. The legacy call then runs with an already-cancelled or soon-cancelled context. The goroutine also uses `obj`, `objInfo` and `options` after the handler has returned, so the caller may still be mutating them.
findings.title: Async legacy writes inherit the request context, which is cancelled when the handler returns

findings.consequence: Storage failures are counted as legacy errors. Legacy DeleteCollection results are counted as storage results. Dashboards and alerts built on these metrics are wrong.
findings.explanation: When Storage.Create or Storage.Update fails, the code calls `recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)`, which is the legacy metric. The DeleteCollection goroutine times the legacy call but reports it with `recordStorageDuration`.
findings.title: Storage and legacy duration metrics are mixed up

findings.consequence: Metric label cardinality grows with every deleted object name, and delete metrics are split across labels that don't match the other methods. Logs from lower layers lack the request fields.

findings.consequence: A null rawTokenId is accepted. encodeTokenId then builds a token id ending in ":null", and getRawTokenId() can return null. This produces malformed token ids instead of failing early.
findings.explanation: The AccessTokenContext constructor calls Objects.requireNonNull(grantType, "Null rawTokenId not allowed") a second time. It never checks rawTokenId, so the null guard for rawTokenId is missing.

findings.consequence: Tokens from the client credentials grant, legacy token exchange, UMA and implicit/hybrid flows carry the wrong grant-type marker in their IDs. Consumers or tests that expect a grant-specific token ID for those grants will fail or misclassify the tokens.
findings.explanation: The change sets Constants.GRANT_TYPE only in createTokenResponse (authorization code, device, CIBA), the resource owner password grant, pre-authorized code, standard token exchange and refresh. TokenManager.initToken calls DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider.getTokenContextFromClientSessionContext, which falls back to UNKNOWN ("na") when the attribute is missing. Grep over services/src/main/java shows no GRANT_TYPE assignment before AccessTokenResponseBuilder.generateAccessToken() in ClientCredentialsGrantType (line 140), AbstractTokenExchangeProvider (line 410), AuthorizationTokenService (UMA, line 358) or OIDCLoginProtocol (line 272). The same applies to the direct createClientAccessToken calls in PolicyEvaluationService and KeycloakIdentity. Client credentials, legacy and V1 token exchange, and UMA tokens therefore get an "na" grant-type segment in their token ID. This is inconsistent…
findings.title: GRANT_TYPE not set on several paths that mint access tokens, so token IDs get "na"

findings.consequence: The event assertions in expectCodeToToken, expectRefresh, expectDeviceCodeToToken and expectAuthReqIdToToken give false confidence. Token IDs encoded with the wrong grant shortcut would pass undetected. If the offset were fixed without fixing the inversion, the tests would fail for correct tokens.
findings.explanation: In isAccessTokenId, the line `if (items[0].substring(3, 5).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;` has two defects. First, the condition is inverted: it rejects a token ID whose grant shortcut matches the expected one. Second, the offset is wrong. Token IDs look like `ofrtro:5678` or `trltcc:1234`, which are 2 chars of session type, 2 of token type and 2 of grant. The grant shortcut is therefore at index 4 to 6, not 3 to 5. substring(3,5) returns the last char of the token-type pair plus the first char of the grant pair, for example `tr`. It will practically never equal a 2-char shortcut, so the inverted check never fires. The matcher therefore only verifies the `xxxxxx:<uuid>` shape and never verifies the grant type. A short prefix (fewer than 5 chars before the colon) also makes substring throw StringIndexOutOfBoundsException instead of returning a mismatch.
findings.title: isAccessTokenId matcher never checks the grant shortcut: condition inverted and offset wrong

findings.consequence: A failing delete leaves a runaway thread that keeps hitting the shared server and can disturb later tests. A late exception from the reader can go unnoticed, which makes the test flaky or weaker than intended.
findings.explanation: The test starts a background reader thread (lines 139-149). It sets `deletedAll` only after all deletes succeed (line 155), and it does not use try/finally. It also never joins the thread before asserting on `caughtExceptions` (line 157). Two things go wrong. First, if any `remove()` call throws, `deletedAll` is never set, so the reader thread loops forever and keeps querying the server. Second, if the reader is in the middle of a request when `deletedAll` is set, an exception from that last request can be added after the assertion has already run. The race this test is meant to catch can therefore be missed.
findings.title: Reader thread in createMultiDeleteMultiReadMulti is never joined and is not stopped on failure

findings.consequence: The resize_emoji job raises ArgumentError whenever it runs, so emoji are no longer resized. The width/height `downsize` overload is dead code.

findings.consequence: Users who follow the unsubscribe link more than once, or whose mail client prefetches links, end up with the topic muted instead of at regular. Users without a TopicUser row get a server error instead of the unsubscribe page. State changes on a GET request are also exposed to link prefetchers.
findings.explanation: The unsubscribe action, served on GET, toggles the notification level. A level above regular is set to regular. Any level at or below regular, including regular itself, is set to muted. Loading the link once from a watching level lowers it to regular. A reload, an email-client link prefetch, or a second click then mutes the topic. TopicUser.find_by can also return nil for a user with no TopicUser row for the topic, such as a user who was emailed but never visited. In that case tu.notification_level raises NoMethodError and returns a 500.
findings.title: GET unsubscribe action is non-idempotent and can crash on missing TopicUser

findings.consequence: The intended omission of website_name for users without a website does not happen. The visible impact is small: the template's {{#if model.website_name}} still treats null as false.
findings.explanation: The serializer's conditional-attribute convention is include_<attr>?, as in include_email? and include_card_image_badge_id? in the same file. The new method is named include_website_name without the '?', so the serializer never calls it. website_name is therefore always serialized. When the website is blank, website_name returns nil early, so the payload carries "website_name": null instead of omitting the key.
findings.title: include_website_name is missing the trailing '?' so it is never called

findings.consequence: Admins see a phantom extra page with no members for groups whose member count is a multiple of the page size. The page indicator also shows one too many pages.
findings.explanation: totalPages is computed as Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1. With user_count=50 and limit=50 it returns 2, but only one page exists. On page 1, showingLast (currentPage == totalPages) is false, so the Next button stays enabled. The `next` action then sets offset to min(0+50, 50) = 50 and calls findMembers(). That fetches an empty page, and currentPage becomes 2. The same off-by-one affects any count that divides evenly by the limit.
findings.title: totalPages overcounts by one when user_count is an exact multiple of limit, so Next loads an empty page

findings.consequence: For any group whose member count is an exact multiple of the page size, the pager shows a phantom extra page. Clicking next shows an empty member list.
findings.explanation: findMembers clamps the offset with Math.min(offset, user_count), so offset == user_count is allowed and returns zero members. The admin-group controller's totalPages is floor(user_count/limit)+1. With 50 members and limit 50, that gives 2 pages. showingLast is false on page 1, so "next" sets offset to min(0+50, 50) = 50 and loads an empty member list.
findings.title: Pagination permits an empty page past the last member when user_count is a multiple of limit

prs.title: FIX: proper handling of group memberships

findings.consequence: A payload with a `*_ids` entry that isn't side-loaded produces an array containing undefined, and the original ids are discarded. Consumers iterating the array then fail on the undefined items, or silently lose data. A null `*_ids` value throws during hydration.
findings.explanation: Hydration only runs when root.__rest_serializer === "1", so it doesn't touch every object. But the new plural branch differs from the singular branch. It maps each id through _lookupSubType, which returns undefined when the id is missing from the side-loaded collection, or when Category.findById finds nothing. Those undefined values stay in the resulting array. `hydrated || []` never applies, because an array is always truthy. The code then deletes the original `*_ids` field regardless, so the unresolved ids are lost. The singular branch only deletes the id when the lookup succeeds. If obj[k] is null or not an array, `.map` throws.
findings.title: Plural *_ids hydration keeps undefined entries and drops the ids unconditionally

findings.consequence: On sites with no `embed_category` row, `rake db:migrate` fails at this migration, so the upgrade is blocked. The `embeddable_hosts` table creation fails with it, because the table creation and the data copy are in the same migration. Separately, the `INSERT` interpolates raw host strings into SQL, so a host value containing a quote will break the statement or inject SQL.
findings.explanation: The migration looks up the category with `execute("SELECT c.id FROM categories AS c INNER JOIN site_settings AS s ON s.value = c.name WHERE s.name = 'embed_category'")[0]['id'].to_i`. `site_settings` only has a row for a setting that an admin has changed from its default. On a site that never set `embed_category`, or whose value matches no category name, the join returns zero rows. `[0]` is then nil and `nil['id']` raises NoMethodError. The `if category_id == 0` fallback is written to handle this case, but it can't run because the exception comes first. The same unguarded `[0]['value']` pattern is on the fallback query.
findings.title: Migration crashes with nil error when no embed_category setting row exists
